turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Hi, I'm Avery, IN DEMAND's AI screening assistant. This is a short first conversation, about ten to fifteen minutes, about the Electrical Engineering Supervisor role in Edmonton. It's recorded so Stefanie's team can review it personally. AI assists the screening, but it doesn't replace human judgment, and you can ask to speak with a person at any time. Shall we start?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Hi Avery, thanks, and yes, let's get started. I appreciate you letting me know it's recorded and that a person reviews it. Just so you have the quick picture, I'm a senior electrical engineer with 14 years in industrial work, a P.Eng. with APEGA for nine years, and I currently lead a team of five at an oil and gas processing facility. I'm looking to move into formal people leadership with more project ownership, so this role caught my eye.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That makes sense. You've already covered what's prompting the move, so I'll go straight to your current role. Could you give me a quick snapshot of the scope you own there, including the kinds of systems and projects your team handles?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Sure. I lead a team of five, three engineers, an engineer-in-training and a designer, covering electrical design and project support for the processing facility. That includes 600-volt motor control centres and variable frequency drives, PLC and control upgrades, and Class I Division 2 area classification reviews under the Canadian Electrical Code and API 500 and 505. On the project side, I redesigned an MCC lineup and VFD upgrade for a gas plant that saved three weeks of a six-week shutdown and finished 4 percent under a 1.8 million dollar budget. I also led a PLC migration on a compressor station, where I wrote the commissioning plan myself. On the quality side, I stamp about 40 drawing sets a year and personally review each one before it goes out.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Okay, the MCC and VFD redesign sounds like a solid result. You've covered a lot of ground there, so I'll pick up with grounding and bonding. What was your part in grounding and bonding design on those power systems?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: On the MCC and VFD work, grounding and bonding was part of the design package, and I was responsible for it under the Canadian Electrical Code. That covered the equipment bonding and ground bus arrangement in the lineup, and proper grounding and shielding for the VFD output cabling. Because I review and stamp the drawing sets personally, I checked those details against the code before anything went out. I don't want to overstate it, though. The stories I've told you are the ones where I owned the overall design, not a standalone grounding study. If this role leans heavily on something like a ground grid design, I'd like to hear how much of that it involves.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That's a good one for Stefanie. She'll confirm it with you. Now, on the hands-on side, what has your direct involvement been with programmable logic controllers, HMIs, and instrumentation and controls?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: On the PLC side, my most direct work was the migration on a compressor station, where I wrote the commissioning plan myself and was involved through startup. HMI and instrumentation work has mostly come through that kind of project, where I handled the electrical and controls design and reviewed the I/O and drawings, while my team and the controls specialists handled a good deal of the detailed programming. So I'm hands-on enough to lead the scope, review it critically, and sign off on it, but I'd describe myself as a design and project lead on controls rather than a full-time programmer. Could you tell me whether this role expects hands-on programming, or more oversight of controls scope?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Of course, we'll make time for your questions at the end. Can you tell me about a time you developed an engineer-in-training, programmer or designer on your team?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Yes, two examples. I mentored an engineer-in-training through her P.Eng. application with APEGA. I helped her line up project experience that matched the competency areas, reviewed her write-ups, and ran practice sessions before her interview, and she passed on her first attempt. The second was a designer who was underperforming on drawing quality and turnaround. I sat down with him, wrote a plan with specific expectations and weekly check-ins, and he improved within about two months. In both cases, what mattered most was being clear on expectations and following up consistently.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That makes sense. Can you tell me about a project you took from estimate or proposal through to commissioning, and what you owned along the way?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: The best example is the MCC lineup and VFD upgrade at the gas plant. I developed the design approach and the scope, and I worked out a shutdown sequence that cut three weeks from a six-week window. I personally reviewed and stamped the drawing sets, coordinated with construction and operations on the outage plan, and followed the work through commissioning. We finished 4 percent under the 1.8 million dollar budget. I'll be upfront that the original cost estimate was built with input from our project controls group, so I owned the technical basis and the budget performance, but I wasn't the sole author of the estimate. Does this role have supervisors owning the estimate and proposal stage, or does that sit with a project manager?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That makes sense, and I'll note your questions on the estimate stage and on programming for the end. Are you legally eligible to work in Canada?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Yes, I'm a Canadian citizen, so I'm fully eligible to work in Canada with no sponsorship needed. I'm also based in Edmonton and not looking to relocate.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Okay, that's clear. You already mentioned your APEGA registration, so I'll move on. Do you hold a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Yes, I hold a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from a Canadian university. That's also the foundation for my P.Eng. with APEGA, which has been in good standing for nine years.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Good. The role involves up to twenty percent travel, with site stays of up to two weeks. Does that work for you?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Yes, that works for me. Up to 20 percent travel is fine, and site stays of up to two weeks are workable too. I'm based in Edmonton, so I'd just plan ahead with my family and team for the longer stretches. Is the travel mostly to client sites, and is it spread fairly evenly through the year or concentrated around project milestones?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Okay, I'll add the travel question to your list for the end. You've mentioned you're based in Edmonton, so what are your salary expectations for a role like this?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I'm expecting a base salary in the range of 165 to 180 thousand dollars for a role like this. I'm open to discussing it once I understand the full scope, the bonus structure, and the benefits. Could you tell me what pay band has been set for the position?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Noted, thank you. Compensation details aren't something I have, so that's a good one for Stefanie. She'll confirm it with you. What notice period would you need to give your current employer?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I'd need to give four weeks' notice to my current employer. I'd want to use that time for a clean handover, particularly for the projects my team has in flight, so I leave them in good shape. If there's a specific start date you're working toward, I'm happy to talk through how that lines up.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That makes sense. I don't have a target start date, so that's a good one for Stefanie. She'll confirm it with you. What questions do you have for me about the role?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Thanks, Avery. I've raised a few along the way, so to pull them together for Stefanie: who the client is, and what the pay band is for the role. I'd also like to know whether the supervisor owns the estimate and proposal stage or whether that sits with a project manager, and how much hands-on PLC programming is expected versus oversight of controls scope. Last, if grounding design like ground grids is a big part of the work, I'd like to understand how much. For next steps, what should I expect on timing after Stefanie's team reviews this?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: The client's name isn't shared, and the pay band, who owns the estimate stage, how much hands-on programming is expected, the ground grid work, and the timing after review are all good ones for Stefanie. She'll confirm them with you. Travel is to industrial project sites, but how it's spread through the year is hers to confirm too. Do you have any other questions for me?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: No, that covers everything for now, Avery. Thanks for walking me through it. I'm looking forward to hearing from Stefanie, and I'm happy to follow up with anything else her team needs, like references or more detail on any of the projects we discussed.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Thank you for your time today. Stefanie's team will review everything personally and be in touch. Take care.

turns.text: Hi, I'm Avery, IN DEMAND's AI screening assistant. This is a short first conversation, about ten to fifteen minutes, about the Electrical Engineering Supervisor role in Edmonton. turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Yes, that sounds good, thanks Avery. I'm happy to get started whenever you are.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Great. What's prompting you to consider a move right now?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Well, I've been at my current consulting firm for a while now, and I've kind of hit a plateau. I like the work, but there isn't really a clear path to grow into a formal leadership role there. I'm hoping a supervisor position would let me build on what I've been doing with the junior engineers, and I'm willing to relocate to Edmonton from Calgary for the right fit.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That makes sense. Could you give me a quick snapshot of your current role and scope?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Sure. I'm a project engineer at a consulting firm in Calgary, and most of my work is electrical design for industrial clients, mainly power distribution and some motor control centres. I'm the project lead on a lot of our jobs, and I have two junior engineers I work with day to day, though I don't have a formal supervisor title. One project I'm proud of was a 4160 volt substation upgrade, where we handled the design and coordinated with the client through construction. I've been a P.Eng. with APEGA for about three years now.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Okay, the substation upgrade sounds like a good one. What hands-on work have you done with programmable logic controllers, HMIs, and instrumentation and controls?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Honestly, that's a lighter area for me. On most of my projects I work with the controls team, so they handle the PLC programming and HMI side, and I focus on the power side, like the single lines, load lists, and how the MCCs tie into the control scheme. I've reviewed I/O lists and control drawings for things like motor starters and interlocks, but I haven't programmed PLCs myself. I'd be upfront that I'd have some learning to do there if the role needs someone hands-on.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That's clear, thanks for being straightforward. Have you worked in hazardous locations, and how did you apply the Canadian Electrical Code or the API 500 and 505 classification standards?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I haven't led a hazardous-location design myself. I've reviewed other people's work on a few projects where there were classified areas, mostly checking that equipment selection and wiring methods lined up with the area classification drawings and the Canadian Electrical Code requirements. I know the basics of the zone and division approach, but I haven't done a classification myself, and I'd be going on general familiarity with API 500 and 505 rather than applying them directly. If that's a big part of the role, I'd want to get up to speed quickly.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Understood. Which drawings or deliverables have you reviewed, authenticated and stamped as a professional engineer under APEGA?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I stamp the electrical design drawings for my projects, so things like single line diagrams, power distribution layouts, and MCC arrangement drawings. Before I stamp, we do an internal review, and I go through the calculations and check the drawings against the design basis and the code requirements. I also review some of the junior engineers' work before it goes out. I'll admit I'm more comfortable describing what I do than laying out every step of the formal process, but I do take the responsibility of the stamp seriously.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Okay, that's helpful. Can you tell me about a time you developed an engineer-in-training, programmer or designer?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: One of the junior engineers I work with came in about a year and a half ago, and I tried to give her room to take on more as she got comfortable. On a smaller MCC project, I had her draft the load list and the single line, and we sat down together to go over her calculations and talk through why certain choices were made. She ended up presenting the design to the client toward the end, which was a good step for her. I'd say it was more informal mentoring than a structured development plan, but it's the part of my work I enjoy most.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That makes sense. Can you tell me about a project you took from estimate or proposal through to commissioning, and what you owned?

turns.speaker: candidate

I'd say I owned the electrical design and the client communication, but the budget and schedule were more managed by our project manager, and I'd have to be careful not to overstate my part in those.

turns.speaker: interviewer

turns.speaker: candidate

turns.speaker: candidate

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That makes sense. The role involves up to twenty percent travel, with site stays of up to two weeks. Does that work for you?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Yes, that works for me. Up to 20 percent travel is fine, and I'm okay with site stays of up to two weeks. Could I ask if the role is remote or hybrid, or if it's mostly in the Edmonton office? And how big is the team I'd be supervising?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Good to know. We'll make time for your questions at the end. What are your salary expectations for a role like this?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I'm looking for something in the range of 140 to 155 thousand dollars. I'm open to talking about the full package too, so if there's flexibility depending on how the role is structured, I'd be glad to hear more.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Noted, thank you. What's your notice period with your current firm?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I'd need about three weeks' notice with my current firm. If there's a relocation to Edmonton involved, I might need a bit of time around that too, but I can work through that based on the start date you have in mind.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That makes sense. Those are all the questions I have, so what questions do you have for me?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Thanks, Avery. I'd like to know how big the team is that I'd be supervising, and whether they're mostly engineers, designers, or a mix. turns.speaker: candidate

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Thank you for your time today. Stefanie's team will review everything personally and follow up with you. Take care.

turns.speaker: candidate

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That makes sense. Could you give me a quick snapshot of your current role and scope?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I'm a junior engineer right now, and before that I was an electrical technologist. We mostly install and troubleshoot motor control centres, and we've done some PLC changes under supervision. I've also coordinated some contractors.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Okay, thanks for that. Which industrial power systems have you been responsible for, such as three-phase distribution, variable frequency drives, or grounding and bonding, and what was your part in them?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Mostly the motor control centres, which are three-phase. We've worked around some drives too, but I'm not sure I'd say I was responsible for them. I helped with installs and troubleshooting, and we followed the code on grounding and bonding.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: I see. Could you give me one specific example, what you did and how it turned out?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Sure. We had a motor control centre that kept tripping on one of the feeders, so we did a lot of troubleshooting and eventually found a loose connection. We fixed it and it ran fine after that. I'm not sure I can give much more detail than that.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Understood. Next, what hands-on work have you done with programmable logic controllers, HMIs, and instrumentation and controls?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: We've done some PLC changes under supervision, mostly small edits to existing programs. I've seen HMIs and instrumentation on the jobs, but I haven't really worked on them much myself, so I'm not sure I can say more than that.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That's helpful. Could you give me one specific example, what you did and how it turned out?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: One time we had to change a PLC program so a pump would start after a different condition. I made the edit under supervision, we tested it, and it worked. I'm not sure I remember the exact details beyond that.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Have you worked in hazardous locations, and if so, how did you apply the Canadian Electrical Code or the API 500 and 505 classification standards?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I haven't really worked in hazardous locations myself. We followed the electrical code on jobs, but I can't name specific sections or the API standards, and I'm not sure I'd want to claim more than that.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Fair enough. Have you reviewed, authenticated, or stamped any drawings or deliverables as a professional engineer under APEGA?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: No, I haven't stamped any drawings. I'm an engineer-in-training with APEGA, not a professional engineer, and I don't have a timeline for getting my P.Eng.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That makes sense. Can you tell me about a time you developed an engineer-in-training, programmer, or designer?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I haven't really developed anyone in that way. We worked as a team, and I've coordinated some contractors, but I haven't led or mentored people formally. I'm not sure I have a good example for that.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Okay, I appreciate your honesty. Can you tell me about a project you took from estimate or proposal through to commissioning, and what you owned?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I haven't taken a project from estimate through to commissioning on my own. We were involved in the install and commissioning side on some jobs, but I wasn't doing the estimating or owning the project. I'm not sure I can give you a full example of that.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Understood. Are you legally eligible to work in Canada?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Yes, I'm a Canadian citizen, so I'm eligible to work in Canada. I'm based in Red Deer.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That makes sense. Do you hold a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: No, I don't. I have an electrical engineering technology diploma, and I'm an engineer-in-training with APEGA.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Okay. I already have your APEGA status, so I won't ask that again. The role involves up to twenty percent travel, with site stays of up to two weeks. Does that work for you?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Yes, travel is fine with me. Two-week site stays wouldn't be a problem.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Good. You mentioned you're based in Red Deer, so does working in Edmonton work for you?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Yes, Edmonton should be fine. I'm not sure yet whether I'd commute or relocate, but it's not a problem for me. Is the role on-site full time, or is there some flexibility?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That's a good one for Stefanie. She'll confirm it with you. What are your salary expectations for a role like this?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I'm expecting around 120 thousand dollars. I'm not sure how that compares to what the role pays, so is there a range you can share?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Noted, thank you. The pay range for this role is a good one for Stefanie, and she'll confirm it with you. What's your notice period with your current employer?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: My notice period is two weeks.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Okay, that's everything I had for you. What questions do you have about the role?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I just have a couple. Is the role really available right away, and what are the next steps in the process? Also, since it's a supervisor role, I'm not sure how my background lines up, so is there anything Stefanie would want me to know about that?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Those are good ones for Stefanie. She'll confirm them with you, including how your background lines up. Do you have any other questions?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: No, that's all for now. Thanks for your time, and I'll wait to hear from Stefanie.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Thank you for your time today. Stefanie's team will review the conversation personally and be in touch. Take care.
